fr:mainmatter.html:p: Cycle through all runnable jobs, giving each a fixed time slice — the stride, time slice, or quantum length — before preempting and moving to the next. The best you can do at minimizing response time: every job sees the CPU within at most N quanta where N is the runnable-job count.
The quantum length is a tradeoff:

html:ul.html:li: Short quantum: better response time, more frequent context switches, worse cache locality.
Long quantum: amortizes context-switch cost, worse response time.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Worst-case response time for N jobs at quantum S is S(N-1).
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Round-robin minimizes response time but is poor for turnaround time relative to STCF scheduling. A scheduler that wants both has to combine ideas — see Multi-level feedback queue.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The scheduler decides which runnable Process to put on the CPU at each moment. There is no single right answer because the metrics conflict:

html:ol.html:li: Turnaround time: time from arrival to completion, T_{\text {completion}} - T_{\text {arrival}}. Minimized by running short jobs first.
Response time: time from arrival to first scheduling. Minimized by frequent rotation.
Fairness: every job makes progress; nobody starves.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: First-in, first-out. Jobs are run to completion in the order they arrive. Trivially fair under any reasonable notion of fairness, but suffers from the convoy effect: a single long-running job at the head delays every shorter job behind it, inflating average turnaround time.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. If the first arriving job is much longer than the rest, all subsequent jobs wait at least its full duration before getting any CPU.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Shortest job first. Run the job with the smallest total work first, run-to-completion. If all jobs arrive at the same time, SJF provably minimizes average turnaround time.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. Real workloads don't all arrive at t = 0. A long job that arrives slightly before a short one still gets to monopolize the CPU until it finishes — SJF degenerates to FIFO scheduling under sequential arrivals.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Removing the run-to-completion constraint and allowing preemption gives STCF scheduling.

Shortest time-to-completion first. A preemptive refinement of SJF scheduling: whenever the scheduler is invoked, it picks the job with the least remaining work. A short job arriving mid-execution can preempt a long one.
STCF is provably optimal for minimizing average turnaround time over all preemptive schedulers.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. Long jobs starve in response time. The lowest-priority work might not get a CPU slice for a very long time, which is unacceptable for interactive workloads.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Cycle through all runnable jobs, giving each a fixed time slice — the stride, time slice, or quantum length — before preempting and moving to the next. The best you can do at minimizing response time: every job sees the CPU within at most N quanta where N is the runnable-job count.
The quantum length is a tradeoff:

html:ul.html:li: Short quantum: better response time, more frequent context switches, worse cache locality.
Long quantum: amortizes context-switch cost, worse response time.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Worst-case response time for N jobs at quantum S is S(N-1).
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Round-robin minimizes response time but is poor for turnaround time relative to STCF scheduling. A scheduler that wants both has to combine ideas — see Multi-level feedback queue.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A practical scheduler that approximates STCF scheduling's turnaround properties and Round-robin scheduling's response properties without requiring foreknowledge of job lengths. Maintain multiple priority queues; within a queue, schedule round-robin. Never service a lower-priority queue while a higher-priority queue has a runnable job.
The priority of a job is not assigned by the user — it is learned from behavior:

html:ul.html:li: New jobs enter at the top priority.
Each priority level has an allotment — the total CPU time a job may consume before being demoted.
Once a job exhausts its allotment at a level, it drops to the next level.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Short jobs that finish quickly never leave the top queue (good turnaround). Interactive jobs that yield often stay at the top (good response time). CPU-bound jobs sink to the bottom and get scheduled when nothing better is runnable.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. Gaming the allotment: a job can issue I/O just before its allotment expires to avoid demotion, since I/O time doesn't count.

html:div.html:details: Solution.Charge the job's allotment for total time at the priority level, including time spent blocked.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. Starvation of low-priority queues if higher queues never empty.

html:div.html:details: Solution.Periodically reset all jobs to the top priority. Cheap and effective.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A proportional-share scheduler. Each runnable job holds some number of tickets, drawn from a fixed total. On each scheduling decision, the scheduler picks a random ticket and runs the job that owns it. Over time, a job receives CPU time proportional to its share of the tickets.
The implementation is trivial: one random number per decision, plus a sum table. No global state about historical CPU usage is needed.
Mechanisms layered on top:

html:ul.html:li: Ticket currency — give each user a fixed number of tickets to split among their processes however they like.
Ticket transfer — a client process can hand tickets to a server to boost its priority while servicing the request.
Ticket inflation — a process can grow its share temporarily, with bounds set by trust.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The unsolved problem is how to assign tickets in the first place. The mechanism is simple; the policy is not.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: A deterministic version of the same idea is Stride scheduling, which avoids the variance of random sampling at the cost of needing global state.

A deterministic proportional-share scheduler. Each job has a stride inversely proportional to its ticket count (the more tickets, the smaller the stride) and a running pass counter that accumulates its stride every time it's scheduled.
The decision is:

html:ol.html:li: Pick the job with the lowest pass.
Increment its pass by its stride.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A job with twice as many tickets has half the stride, so its pass grows half as fast, so it gets scheduled twice as often. Same long-run behavior as Lottery scheduling, but with zero variance.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. New jobs need an initial pass value. Setting it to 0 lets them dominate; setting it to the global minimum lets them merge in cleanly but requires tracking that minimum.
Remark. Each context switch is not free. Choosing a longer time slice amortizes that cost at the price of response time.
Remark. I/O-bound jobs are commonly handled by splitting a job into its non-I/O segments and scheduling them individually — turning one long-but-mostly-blocked job into many short, runnable ones.

fr:title.text: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces: Exercises

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces: Exercises

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Worked homework for Three Easy Pieces, one chapter per chapter of the book. The conceptual material lives in the concept pages — Process, Process API, Process control block for the process abstraction; fork(), wait(), exec(), Unix signals for the process API; FIFO scheduling, SJF scheduling, Round-robin scheduling for the schedulers. Simulator questions are answered twice over: what I predicted before running anything, then what the tool actually printed. The prediction is the experiment, and the ones I got wrong are the entries worth rereading.

fr:title.text: CPU utilization of two compute-bound processes

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: CPU utilization of two compute-bound processes

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Run process-run.py with the flags -l 5:100,5:100. What should the CPU utilization be?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:div:
Prediction. Two processes of 5 instructions each, every instruction using the CPU with probability one, so nothing ever blocks: Process 0 cpu cpu cpu cpu cpu
Process 1 cpu cpu cpu cpu cpu Utilization should be 100%. The first process runs to completion, then the second. Were both waiting on I/O this would not hold.
html:details.html:p: Confirmed with -c -p: 100% utilization.

fr:title.text: Completion time when one process blocks on I/O

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Completion time when one process blocks on I/O

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Run process-run.py with the flags -l 4:100,1:0. How long does it take to complete both processes?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:div:
Prediction. One process of 4 CPU instructions and one of a single I/O instruction: Process 0 cpu cpu cpu cpu
Process 1 io io_done It should take 4 + \text {time of IO}: the compute-bound process runs its four instructions first, and only then does the second process start and sit out the whole I/O.
html:details.html:p: With -c -p it takes 11 timesteps, which is indeed \approx 4 + \text {time of IO}.

fr:title.text: Why the order of the processes matters

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why the order of the processes matters

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Switch the order: ./process-run.py -l 1:0,4:100. What happens now? Does switching the order matter, and why?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:div:
Prediction. Now the trace is Process 0 io io_done
Process 1 cpu cpu cpu cpu which should take \max (5, 1 + \text {time IO}) depending on the -L flag. Order matters, because the CPU instructions can run while the non-blocking I/O is outstanding — which is the argument for scheduling at all.
html:details.html:p: It takes 7 timesteps: the I/O overlaps with the compute as expected.

fr:title.text: SWITCH_ON_END serializes an I/O-bound process against a CPU-bound one

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: SWITCH_ON_END serializes an I/O-bound process against a CPU-bound one

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The -S flag decides how the system reacts when a process issues I/O. Under SWITCH_ON_END the system does not switch away while a process is doing I/O; it waits until that process finishes entirely. What happens with one I/O-bound and one CPU-bound process — -l 1:0,4:100 -c -S SWITCH_ON_END?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:p: The whole CPU-bound process is held hostage by the I/O:

html:pre.html:code: Time PID: 0 PID: 1 CPU IOs 1 RUN:io READY 1 2 BLOCKED READY 1 3 BLOCKED READY 1 4 BLOCKED READY 1 5 BLOCKED READY 1 6 BLOCKED READY 1 7* RUN:io_done READY 1 8 DONE RUN:cpu 1 9 DONE RUN:cpu 1 10 DONE RUN:cpu 1 11 DONE RUN:cpu 1

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Run the same processes with switching set to happen whenever one is WAITING for I/O — -l 1:0,4:100 -c -S SWITCH_ON_IO. What happens now? Use -c and -p to confirm.

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:div: Prediction. Timestep 1 still runs RUN:io, but then PID: 1 should occupy the next 4 timesteps until it completes. After one more BLOCKED step we run RUN:io_done and both finish.
html:details.html:p: Exactly that:

html:pre.html:code: Time PID: 0 PID: 1 CPU IOs 1 RUN:io READY 1 2 BLOCKED RUN:cpu 1 1 3 BLOCKED RUN:cpu 1 1 4 BLOCKED RUN:cpu 1 1 5 BLOCKED RUN:cpu 1 1 6 BLOCKED DONE 1 7* RUN:io_done DONE 1

fr:title.text: IO_RUN_LATER wastes the overlap it just bought

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: IO_RUN_LATER wastes the overlap it just bought

fr:mainmatter.html:p: With -I IO_RUN_LATER, a completed I/O does not immediately return the issuing process to the CPU; whatever was running keeps running. What happens with ./process-run.py -l 3:0,5:100,5:100,5:100 -S SWITCH_ON_IO -I IO_RUN_LATER -c -p? Are system resources being used effectively?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:div: Prediction. They are not. All three CPU-bound processes finish before we return to the I/O-bound one, which then issues its next io with nothing left to overlap it against — the concurrency benefit evaporates.
html:details.html:p: The trace is long, but the totals say it:

html:pre.html:code: Stats: Total Time 31 Stats: CPU Busy 21 (67.74%) Stats: IO Busy 15 (48.39%)

fr:title.text: IO_RUN_IMMEDIATE and why recent I/O predicts more I/O

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: IO_RUN_IMMEDIATE and why recent I/O predicts more I/O

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Run the same processes with -I IO_RUN_IMMEDIATE, which runs the issuing process as soon as its I/O completes. How does the behavior differ, and why might rerunning a process that just finished I/O be a good idea?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:div: Prediction. Returning to the I/O-bound process lets it issue its next io before handing the CPU back, so the requests stay in flight alongside the compute. As a heuristic it is a bet that a process which just did I/O will do more of it.
html:details.html:p: The bet pays:

html:pre.html:code: Stats: Total Time 21 Stats: CPU Busy 21 (100.00%) Stats: IO Busy 15 (71.43%)

fr:title.text: Which flag matters under randomly generated workloads

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Which flag matters under randomly generated workloads

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Run some randomly generated processes — -s 1 -l 3:50,3:50, -s 2 -l 3:50,3:50, -s 3 -l 3:50,3:50. Predict how the trace turns out. What changes between -I IO_RUN_IMMEDIATE and -I IO_RUN_LATER, and between -S SWITCH_ON_IO and -S SWITCH_ON_END?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:div: Prediction. With each instruction a coin flip between CPU and I/O, IO_RUN_LATER and IO_RUN_IMMEDIATE should be close to indistinguishable. SWITCH_ON_IO over SWITCH_ON_END should matter more and more as processes are added, since there is almost always CPU work waiting — though with only two processes the gain may be small, as both are likely to be blocked at some point.
html:details.html:p: For seed -s 1 the two -I policies perform identically, and enabling SWITCH_ON_IO improves both CPU and I/O utilization.

fr:title.text: fork() copies the address space, not the variable

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: fork() copies the address space, not the variable

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Write a program that calls fork(). Before forking, set a variable — say x — to 100. What is its value in the child? What happens when parent and child both change it?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:p: The child gets a copy of the parent's address space, x included. Each subsequent write lands in that process's own copy, so neither sees the other's change.

fr:title.text: A file descriptor survives the fork

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A file descriptor survives the fork

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Open a file with open() and then fork(). Can both child and parent use the returned descriptor? What happens when they write to the file concurrently?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:p: Both have access to the same descriptor. Concurrent writes can in principle interleave, but in my runs whichever process was scheduled first always finished writing before the other started — plausibly a scheduling artifact rather than a guarantee.

fr:title.text: Ordering child before parent without wait()

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Ordering child before parent without wait()

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Write a program where the child prints "hello" and the parent prints "goodbye", with the child always printing first. Can you do it without calling wait() in the parent?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:p: Reusing the shared file from the previous exercise: have the child write a value, and have the parent spin in a while loop until it reads that value back. It works, and it is miserable — which is presumably why wait() exists.

fr:title.text: What wait() returns, and what it does in the child

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What wait() returns, and what it does in the child

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now use wait() in the parent to wait for the child. What does it return? What happens if you call wait() in the child?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:p: It returns the pid of the child that died. Called in the child — which has no children of its own — it returns -1 immediately.

fr:title.text: Why exec() has so many variants

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why exec() has so many variants

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Write a program that calls fork() and then some form of exec() to run /bin/ls. Try the variants — execl(), execle(), execlp(), execv(), execvp(), execvP(). Why are there so many spellings of one call?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:p: The suffixes are a small matrix of three independent choices. The v family takes a variable-size argument vector where the l family takes a fixed argument list. The e family takes an explicit environment — the list of environment variables the new program will see — instead of inheriting the caller's. The p family resolves the program name against PATH, the way a shell does, instead of requiring a path.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Rewrite the previous program using waitpid() instead of wait(). When is waitpid() the one you want?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:p: When a parent has several children. wait() returns on whichever dies first; waitpid() lets you name the child you care about.

fr:title.text: printf() after closing STDOUT in the child

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: printf() after closing STDOUT in the child

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Create a child process that closes standard output (STDOUT_FILENO). What happens if the child then calls printf()?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:p: Nothing prints from the child. The parent's stdout is a separate descriptor and is untouched, so it still prints.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Create two children and connect the standard output of one to the standard input of the other using pipe().

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:p: It worked only once I added fflush() — the writer's output was sitting in stdio's buffer rather than in the pipe. Whether that is required in general or an artifact of how I structured the writer, I am not sure.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The operation of saving the full execution state of one process (or thread) and restoring another's so the CPU can resume it as if it had never been interrupted. On a trap into the kernel, the hardware stashes the user-visible state (PC, condition codes, stack pointer) into a known location, and the OS saves the remaining general-purpose registers as part of the switching code.
Two flavors of state are involved:

html:ol.html:li: User registers: the current program's context (general-purpose registers, stack vars).
Kernel registers: meta-information used to resume the trap correctly (PC at trap, syscall number, etc.).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Context switches are not free — they incur the cost of cache and TLB pollution in addition to the direct cost of saving/restoring state. This is the cost amortized by larger scheduling quanta and a recurring concern for any Concurrency system.
